title: Buy Now Pay Later is 0% Interest, So Why Are People Paying Fees?
summary: Data-driven essay uses Federal Reserve survey results to explain how a zero-interest BNPL plan can still cause a bank overdraft fee.

assertions.quote: 11% of BNPL users said a BNPL payment had triggered an overdraft or NSF fee during the prior year
most pay-in-four providers were not routinely reporting these loans to credit reporting agencies
20% of BNPL users said they had financed groceries or food delivery
89% did not report a BNPL triggered overdraft or NSF fee

verdicts.note: Matches the Federal Reserve's 2025 household survey, where most respondents did not report either outcome, even though a meaningful minority did.
Fed SHED: about 74% of BNPL users were not late on a payment in the prior year, and 89% did not have a payment trigger an overdraft/NSF fee -- a clear majority avoided both problems.

LendingTree: only a slim 53% majority of users say they have NOT paid late in the past year (47% have, another 15% have paid late before but not recently, and 38% say they've never paid late) -- a narrower majority than Fed SHED's 74%.

The inverse of CFPB's late-fee figure: roughly 89-90% of borrowers at the five surveyed lenders were not charged a late fee in 2021, consistent with most users not triggering a late payment or an associated bank fee in a given year.

assertions.quote: only 14% of BNPL users answered both tested questions about credit effects correctly

verdicts.note: Matches Federal Reserve survey data finding only a small share of users answered basic BNPL credit-effect questions correctly.
Fed SHED: 38% of BNPL users wrongly agreed BNPL builds credit history (40% more unsure), 53% wrongly agreed on-time payments help their score, and only 14% answered both questions correctly.

assertions.quote: a buyer with stable income, a known purchase, and enough buffer, four fixed zero interest payments may simply align spending with cash timing
